Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Carlos Carlos, a 58-year-old Latin American man married to his high school sweetheart, has been working as a forensic analyst for over three decades. His meticulous attention to detail and unwavering commitment to justice defined his career until the catastrophic event that forever altered his life. The disaster occurred at the heart of a bustling city, where an explosion ripped through the financial district during rush hour. Carlos was on-site within minutes, part of a team dispatched to gather evidence from the wreckage. The scene was chaos—smoke billowing into the sky, debris scattered everywhere, and the acrid smell of burning materials permeating the air. As he moved through the rubble, he heard faint cries for help and the distant wails of sirens. His job required him to navigate this hazardous terrain with precision, but every step felt like a gamble. In the months following the event, Carlos began to avoid unfamiliar places altogether. The idea of stepping into an unknown environment filled him with dread because he couldn’t assess the danger lurking around each corner. This avoidance extended beyond his professional life; even simple outings to new restaurants or stores became overwhelming challenges. He found himself relying on well-trodden paths and familiar routines, a behavior that isolated him from many social activities he once enjoyed. His startle response was another persistent symptom. Even the gentlest sounds—like a door creaking or a sudden noise outside—made his heart race and his body tense up. His wife, Maria, noticed this and often commented on how jumpy he seemed, but Carlos could not control his reactions. He felt constantly vigilant, as if danger was always just around the corner. Carlos’s self-perception had also shifted dramatically since the disaster. He believed that his reactions post-event demonstrated poor coping skills; every time he flinched or avoided a situation, it reinforced in his mind that he couldn’t handle crises effectively. This sense of inadequacy extended to his professional life as well. The event had left him feeling no longer capable of performing tasks that once defined him. His role as a forensic analyst required a level of composure and focus that he now found difficult to maintain, leading to increased errors and a growing fear of making mistakes on the job. These feelings were compounded by his belief that the world was fundamentally dangerous. The explosion had shattered what he thought was an orderly existence; instead, it revealed a chaotic undercurrent beneath everyday life. This perception affected not only how Carlos viewed the world but also how he interacted with it. He avoided news and conversations about similar disasters, fearing they would reignite his anxiety. The cumulative effect of these symptoms began to strain his relationships. Maria noticed that her husband was increasingly withdrawn and less engaged in their daily activities. They used to explore new neighborhoods together on weekends, trying out different restaurants or attending cultural events. Now, Carlos often declined such outings, citing fatigue or preferring to stay home. His reluctance to participate in shared hobbies left Maria feeling isolated and concerned about his well-being. At work, Carlos’s performance suffered as he struggled with concentration and heightened stress levels. He began making more mistakes in his analyses, which led to increased scrutiny from supervisors. The pressure at work only exacerbated his anxiety, creating a vicious cycle where each perceived failure reinforced his belief that he was no longer capable of performing his job. What finally brought Carlos to seek help was an incident at the office during a particularly tense day. A sudden noise startled him so severely that he nearly dropped a critical piece of evidence he was handling. This moment crystallized for him how debilitating his symptoms had become and how they were impacting both his professional life and his relationship with Maria. Carlos is most afraid of losing control completely, feeling like an incapable person in the eyes of those around him. However, he also hopes that through therapy, he can regain some sense of normalcy and control over his life. He wants to reconnect with Maria and return to a state where he feels competent both at work and within himself. As Carlos begins his journey toward recovery, it is clear that the psychological aftermath of the man-made disaster has profoundly reshaped his worldview and daily experiences. The challenge now lies in helping him navigate these changes while rebuilding his sense of self and security.
